title: Annapolis
full_review:
The plot of director Justin Lin's diverting but derivative "Annapolis" (Touchstone) -- young man tries to prove his mettle while pursuing dream of becoming a Navy officer -- sounds like a good idea for a movie. Just as it did for "An Officer and a Gentleman"!

Bearing some resemblance to young Richard Gere, an appealing James Franco stars as Jake Huard, a scrappy shipyard worker and amateur boxer who, for vague and improbable reasons, is accepted into the prestigious U.S. Naval Academy.

There he is pushed to the limit, as he and his fellow "plebes" (Naval Academy speak for freshman cadets) are put through a rigorous gauntlet of mental and physical tests.

As with these "be all you can be" military melodramas, there is no shortage of instructors who try to break them. It is during these sequences that the echoes of "Officer" are clearest, with Jake at several points declaring defiantly, "I ain't quittin'!" There is a further ripped-off subplot in which Jake helps a struggling classmate make it through a grueling obstacle course.

Though played with more steel-jawed understatement (and fewer expletives) than Louis Gossett Jr.'s tough gunnery sergeant, Tyrese Gibson co-stars as ex-Marine company commander and Jake's chief antagonist, Midshipman Lt. Cole. (Eyes locked in dagger-shooting mode abound!)

The film switches midway from boot camp to boxing ring, as Jake, eager for some payback, prepares to face off against Cole at the academy's annual tournament.

Jordana Brewster also co-stars as Ali, an instructor at the school who becomes Jake's love interest. The inter-rank romance is only one of the implausible story elements. How is it that Jake isn't expelled for blatant bad sportsmanship and attacking a senior officer when another cadet is tossed for merely lying about taking a shower?

Chi McBride and Donnie Wahlberg serve limited duty as a boxing coach and member of the school's brass, respectively.

Apart from some barracks banter, there is relatively little objectionable content, though many viewers may find the intense ring violence off-putting.

Though Lin's adrenalized climax achieves its desired rousing effect, the film is hollow and formulaic. At best, you may want to wait until this adequately entertaining film drops anchor in your video store.

The film contains brutal boxing sequences, an attempted suicide, some sexually crude language and humor, as well as profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
